## Datasets

### Intracranial data

The intracranial EEG data were obtained from the MNI Open iEEG Atlas [@frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial], a normative resource compiled from 106 patients with refractory epilepsy recorded at three centres. Only channels implanted in brain regions that were determined to be non-epileptogenic throughout the monitoring period were retained, yielding 1772 channels (13 channels were removed from the initial release as they were later judged erroneous on visual inspection) distributed across 38 cortical regions defined by the MICCAI atlas. @fig-frauscher-atlas provides a spatial overview of channel coverage in the atlas, distinguishing depth/stereo-EEG contacts from cortical grid and strip contacts across both hemispheres.

These 38 regions were derived from the consolidation of 20 smaller MICCAI labels into 8 functional groups to ensure sufficient channel density (min. 5 per region), while 16 labels were omitted due to lack of coverage. For each channel, 60 seconds of resting wakefulness data with eyes closed were available.

![Spatial distribution of the MNI Open iEEG Atlas channels and regional reference centroids in MNI space. (**A**) Glass-brain visualization of the 1785 intracranial EEG channels, with depth and stereo-EEG contacts shown in blue and cortical grid/strip contacts shown in orange. For visualization, left-hemisphere channel coordinates were assigned negative x-values based on the hemisphere label. (**B**) Glass-brain visualization of the regional reference centroids used in the grouped regional analyses, shown as enlarged magenta markers.](figures/chapter2/frauscher_channels_and_centroids.png){#fig-frauscher-atlas fig-align="center" width="80%"}

Signals were band-pass filtered at 0.5–80 Hz and resampled to 200 Hz. Power spectral density (PSD) was estimated using Welch's method with 2-second Hamming windows and 50% overlap, resulting in a frequency resolution of 0.5 Hz. Spectral densities were normalised to unit total power, making them independent of signal amplitude. Full preprocessing details are given in @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial.

### Reconstructed sources

5 minutes of eyes-open resting-state EEG data were collected in 19 healthy young adult volunteers (age 28 ± 6 years, 14 females) with Ethics Committee of ETH Zurich approval. EEG signals were recorded at 1000 Hz sampling rate using a 256-channel HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net by Electrical Geodesics (Eugene, Oregon, USA). The full details of collecting and preprocessing this dataset were described in @samogin2019SharedConnectionspecificIntrinsic and @samogin2020FrequencydependentFunctionalConnectivity. Poor channels were identified (0–13 per subject) and interpolated, data were band-pass filtered within 1–80 Hz, and biological artefacts were removed using fixed-point ICA (FastICA). The realistic head model was provided as input to the exact low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (eLORETA) algorithm [@pascual-marqui2011AssessingInteractionsBrain], together with the preprocessed EEG signals, to estimate brain activity in source space at high temporal resolution.

While the HD-EEG data were recorded with eyes open, the following steps were chosen to match the iEEG atlas. Source activity was extracted from reconstructed sources using average coordinates from the electrodes within 76 MICCAI-defined ROIs in MNI space, resulting in 1444 virtual sensors, with the grouped regional reference coordinates illustrated in @fig-frauscher-atlas, panel B. For every virtual sensor, 60 s of activity was extracted, downsampled to 200 Hz to match the iEEG sampling rate. Spectral densities were computed using identical Welch parameters (2 s windows, 50% overlap, 0.5 Hz resolution).

All spectral data were normalised to unit total power to ensure that the comparison focused on the distribution of frequency peaks (e.g. the occipital alpha or hippocampal delta) rather than absolute amplitude differences between scalp and intracranial sensors.

## Shared spectral methods

<!-- [VERIFY: confirm the fitting range used in the production runs. Intro says "0.5-80 Hz or 1-80 Hz"; aperiodic_paper.qmd uses 0.5-80. Pick one and use it throughout.] -->

All specparam fits in this chapter use the following settings: peak width limits [1, 8] Hz, maximum number of peaks 8, peak threshold 3.0 (in units of standard deviation of the residual), fitting range 0.5–80 Hz. The aperiodic mode (knee vs fixed) is selected per modality on the basis of BIC and prior evidence, and is reported in §Stage 3 below; downstream stages that rely on specparam outputs use the model selected there. Model fit quality is summarised by R²; channels with R² below 0.9 are flagged and the sensitivity of regional results to their inclusion is reported. For each channel and region, the parameters of interest are the aperiodic offset $b$, exponent $\chi$, and (for the knee model) knee parameter $k$, together with the centre frequency, power, and bandwidth of each parametrised peak.

For each modality, spectral parameters are aggregated within atlas regions. For the iEEG atlas, parameters are averaged across all channels assigned to each of the 38 MICCAI regions. For the HD-EEG dataset, parameters are first computed per subject per label and then averaged across subjects to produce group-level regional estimates. Cross-modal correspondence is quantified using Spearman rank correlations across regions, with significance assessed by permutation testing (10 000 permutations, shuffling region labels) to account for the small number of spatial units.

## Stage 1 — Phenomenological description of regional oscillatory features

### Methods

#### Frauscher-style k-means clustering

To enable direct comparison with the original atlas, the peak-detection procedure of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial was reproduced. The normalised power spectra were classified into $k$ groups using the k-means algorithm, with 160 features corresponding to the frequency steps from 0.5 to 80 Hz in 0.5 Hz increments, using Euclidean distance and 100 repetitions. The classification was repeated with increasing $k$ until a group without peaks was identified, defined as the group whose mean normalised spectrum was lower than the maximum among the other groups. The 50% of channels closest to the group mean were retained as the no-peak set.

The 160 frequency bins were grouped into 22 frequency intervals based on the condition that each bin contains at least 4% of total mean power, yielding boundaries at 0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 3.25, 3.75, 4.25, 5.25, 6.25, 6.75, 7.75, 8.25, 9.25, 10.25, 11.75, 13.25, 15.25, 17.25, 20.25, 24.25, 31.75, and 80 Hz. The presence of a peak in a given frequency interval for a particular brain region was determined by comparing the distribution of spectral densities of all channels in that region against the distribution of the no-peak set at the same interval, using a one-sided two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test at the 5% significance level with Dunnett's correction for multiple comparisons across 42 regions (38 cortical regions plus 4 lobes) and 22 frequency intervals.

For the HD-EEG data the same procedure was applied with the iEEG-derived frequency intervals retained for comparability, even though the 4% power condition was not met for the source-reconstructed spectra. The implications of this deviation are reported below as a finding of Stage 1.



### Results

#### Cluster solutions

The k-means clustering procedure applied to the iEEG atlas yielded eight spectral groups, closely matching the original classification reported by @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial. Seven groups were characterised by prominent peaks in one or more canonical frequency bands (delta, theta, alpha, low beta, high beta, gamma, and mixed), while one group — the no-peak set — exhibited a smooth, monotonically decreasing spectrum with no visible narrowband peaks. The overall structure of these clusters was highly similar to the published result, although the absolute scaling of normalised spectral density differed slightly. The no-peak set served as the reference distribution for all subsequent peak-detection tests.

Applying the same procedure to the HD-EEG source-reconstructed data yielded six spectral groups. The reduced number of clusters indicates a narrower range of spectral shapes than in iEEG, consistent with the spatial smoothing introduced by source reconstruction. The HD-EEG no-peak cluster had a flatter profile than its iEEG counterpart, with stronger concentration of power in the alpha range across most clusters, likely reflecting both the eyes-open recording condition and the dominance of posterior sources in the source model. @fig-ieeg-clusters presents these clustering results side by side.

![Spectral clustering in iEEG and HD-EEG source-reconstructed data. Panel A shows the eight iEEG clusters and Panel B shows the six HD-EEG clusters. In both modalities, one no-peak cluster is visible. HD-EEG shows more clusters, most of them distinguished only by the average power of the alpha peak. In the iEEG clusters, the knee is visible; reconstructed sources have more straightforward 1/f-like characteristics.](figures/chapter2/combined_clusters_psd.svg){#fig-ieeg-clusters width="100%" column="page"}

The 22 frequency intervals proposed by @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial were defined so that each bin contained at least 4% of total mean power in the iEEG data. This condition was not satisfied for the source-reconstructed spectra, where power was more concentrated in the alpha range and the higher-frequency bins fell below the 4% threshold. The clustering result and the cluster identities themselves were also sensitive to the chosen fitting range: small changes in the upper or lower bound of the fit altered both the cluster solution and the contents of the no-peak set. The instability is reported here as a finding of Stage 1 rather than as a nuisance, and motivates the parallel use of the more stable per-band parametrised-peak descriptor below.

## Stage 2 — Cross-modal correspondence on uncorrected spectra

### Methods

Cross-modal agreement between the iEEG atlas and the source-reconstructed HD-EEG was quantified using the band-overlap metric of @afnan2024ValidationMEGSource, applied directly to the unit-power-normalised PSDs. Channels were pooled across hemispheres by grouping on the hemisphere-agnostic MICCAI region name, collapsing left and right ROIs into the 38 bilateral regions of the atlas. Within each region $r$, the iEEG atlas was taken as the reference modality and the HD-EEG source data as the estimated modality. Let $\widetilde{L}_r(f)$ denote the median of the log-PSD across the channels of region $r$ at frequency bin $f$, and $\text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)$ the corresponding standard deviation in HD-EEG. The bin-wise overlap is

$$\text{overlap}_r(f) = \begin{cases} 1 - \dfrac{\bigl\lvert \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{iEEG}}_r(f) - \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)\bigr\rvert}{\text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)}, & \bigl\lvert \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{iEEG}}_r(f) - \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)\bigr\rvert \le \text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \\[2mm] 0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$

The metric equals 1 when the iEEG median lands exactly on the HD-EEG median and decreases linearly to 0 once the two medians differ by one HD-EEG standard deviation. The bin-wise overlap was averaged across the frequency bins of each canonical band ($\delta$ 0.5–4, $\theta$ 4–8, $\alpha$ 8–13, $\beta$ 13–30, $\gamma$ 30–80 Hz), yielding one value per region per band. Both the unaveraged bin-level overlap and the band-averaged summary are reported.

## Stage 3 — Aperiodic component modelled and removed

### Methods

#### Model selection: knee vs fixed by BIC

Specparam was fit in both knee and fixed aperiodic modes to each modality over the shared fitting range, using the shared peak settings. The aperiodic mode for downstream analyses was selected per modality on the basis of the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), with the model achieving the lower BIC retained. Because the knee model carries one extra parameter and BIC penalises model complexity, this selection is reported alongside prior evidence on the spectral shape of each modality. The iEEG atlas exhibits a clear knee in log-log space as originally reported by @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial and consistent with reports that knees are commonly observed in intracranial recordings [@donoghue2024EvaluatingComparingMeasures; @bush2024AperiodicComponentsLocal]. HD-EEG source-reconstructed spectra are typically near-linear in log-log space across the fitted range, where the fixed model is the standard choice [@donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower].

#### Aperiodic subtraction

The fitted aperiodic component was reconstructed on the fitted frequency grid and subtracted from the empirical PSD in linear power space, yielding the residual

$$\text{PSD}_\text{osc}(f) = \text{PSD}(f) - \text{PSD}_\text{ap}(f).$$

This is the primary residual used throughout Stage 3. A log-ratio alternative, $L_\text{osc}(f) = \log_{10}\bigl(\text{PSD}(f) / \text{PSD}_\text{ap}(f)\bigr)$, corresponding to the specparam convention, is reported as a sensitivity comparison where time permits.

In knee mode, the aperiodic component is modelled in log-power space as

$$L_\text{ap}(f) = b - \log_{10}\bigl(k + f^{\chi}\bigr),$$

where $b$ is the offset, $k$ the knee parameter, and $\chi$ the exponent governing the high-frequency roll-off. In fixed mode,

$$L_\text{ap}(f) = b - \chi \cdot \log_{10}(f).$$


#### specparam-based peak prevalence per band

Decide before writing the result.] -->

Specparam fits were extracted using the shared settings above. For each channel, parametrised peaks were assigned to the canonical bands $\delta$ (0.5–4 Hz), $\theta$ (4–8 Hz), $\alpha$ (8–13 Hz), $\beta$ (13–30 Hz), and $\gamma$ (30–80 Hz) according to their centre frequency. Peak prevalence in a region was defined as the proportion of channels in that region exhibiting at least one peak in a given band. The procedure operates on the same channel-to-region assignment as the clustering analysis above.

#### Survival of clustering-based and peak-prevalence findings after correction

The Frauscher peak-detection procedure (k-means, no-peak set, KS test) and the specparam peak-prevalence procedure were both re-applied to the aperiodic-corrected spectra. For each region × frequency interval combination from the clustering procedure, and each region × canonical band combination from the peak-prevalence procedure, the presence of a significant peak before correction was compared with the presence of a significant peak after correction. Peaks that survived correction were considered robust against the aperiodic background; peaks that disappeared after correction were considered potentially confounded by aperiodic variation.

## Stage 4 — Stability of aperiodic features

### Methods

#### Knee vs fixed exponent rank agreement

For each modality, the channel-level exponent estimated under the knee model was compared with the channel-level exponent estimated under the fixed model. Because the two exponents are not on the same scale, the comparison was made by rank correlation across channels (Pearson and Spearman) rather than by direct numerical agreement.

#### Stability of the fixed-mode exponent across fitting ranges

For each modality, the fixed-mode exponent was computed twice: once over 1–80 Hz and once over 1–45 Hz. The per-channel agreement between the two estimates was quantified. These comparisons were pooled into a hierarchical Bayesian regression with the exponent as the outcome, fitting range as a fixed-effect predictor, modality as a fixed-effect predictor, and ROI and subject as random effects, to localise where the choice of fitting range materially shifts the estimate.

<!-- [PLACEHOLDER: specify the Bayesian model formula, priors, sampler, convergence diagnostics. Implementation pending.] -->

#### IRASA vs specparam exponent at matched band

As a complementary check, the aperiodic exponent in HD-EEG was estimated using Irregular Resampling Auto-Spectral Analysis (IRASA; @wen2016SeparatingFractalOscillatory). IRASA computes the power spectrum at multiple resampling factors ($h$ = 1.05 to 2.0 in steps of 0.05); for each factor, the geometric mean of the up-sampled and down-sampled spectra is taken, and the median across factors yields the fractal (aperiodic) component. Because IRASA up-samples the signal by up to $h_\text{max} = 2$, the analysed band is bounded by the Nyquist limit, $h_\text{max} \cdot f_\text{hi} < f_s / 2$. With $f_s = 200$ Hz this restricts the upper edge to below 50 Hz, so the IRASA decomposition was run over 2–40 Hz. The fractal exponent was obtained by fitting a line in log-log space to the IRASA aperiodic spectrum; the sign-reversed slope gives the IRASA exponent. For direct comparison, specparam was additionally refit in fixed mode over the same 2–40 Hz band, and the per-channel exponents from the two methods were compared by Pearson and Spearman correlation.
